title: Scaling and Condensation of Dry Active Matter Around Circular Obstacles
authors: Felipe P. S. Júnior, F. Q. Potiguar, Jorge L. C. Domingos, W. P. Ferreira
abstract: Active Brownian particles confined to rigid substrates are known to accumulate near rigid boundaries and, under suitable conditions, undergo motility-induced phase separation (MIPS). A particularly intriguing manifestation of this behavior is the formation of self-sustained vortices around circular obstacles, which act as localized nucleation sites for particle aggregation. While several dynamical properties of such vortices have been previously characterized, their behavior in the thermodynamic limit remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate how the mass and spatial extent of a dry active-matter vortex scale with system size. Using numerical simulations of repulsive active Brownian Particles interacting with a fixed circular obstacle, we measure the vortex mass, mean radius, and maximum radius as functions of the global area fraction, obstacle size, and system size. We find two distinct scaling regimes. At low densities, the vortex remains localized and its characteristic properties saturate as the system size increases. Above a critical density, however, the vortex mass grows extensively with the total number of particles, while its spatial dimensions scale linearly with the system size, indicating the emergence of an obstacle-stabilized condensed state.
summary: This work studies active matter confined by circular obstacles, finding that the resulting vortices can undergo a phase transition. Below a critical density, the vortex remains localized, but above it, the vortex forms an extensive, obstacle-stabilized condensate. The findings establish a clear link between local geometry and macroscopic phase behavior in active systems.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the mass and spatial extent of self-sustained vortices formed by dry active matter scale with system size, particularly analyzing the transition between localized and extensive condensed states.
main_result: The system exhibits two distinct scaling regimes: at low densities, the vortex is localized, but above a critical density, the vortex mass grows extensively with the total particle number, indicating an obstacle-stabilized condensed state.
method: The study uses numerical simulations of Active Brownian Particles (ABPs) interacting with a fixed circular obstacle, analyzing scaling laws and comparing results to a derived kinetic model.
model_or_system: The system consists of dry active matter particles modeled by an overdamped Langevin equation, interacting via repulsive forces near a circular obstacle. The analysis focuses on the resulting vortex structures and their thermodynamic limit behavior.
key_observables: Vortex mass (M), mean radius (R), maximum radius (R_max), and the scaling exponent ($\alpha$) relating vortex mass to particle number ($M \sim N^\alpha$).
important_parameters: Global area fraction ($\phi$), obstacle size ($D$), system size ($L$), and the critical density ($\phi^*_b$) separating scaling regimes.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes purely repulsive interactions and focuses on the thermodynamic limit behavior of the active system.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the density dependence of vortex mass scaling ($\alpha$ vs $\phi$), the vortex mass fraction ($f_c$ vs $\phi_t$), and the scaling of vortex radii ($R, R_{max}$) with system size ratios ($L/D$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the physical model and observables, establishing the two distinct scaling regimes (low vs. high density), developing a kinetic model to explain the transition, and finally analyzing the geometric properties of the resulting condensate.
why_interesting: The concept of obstacle-stabilized condensation in active matter provides a non-equilibrium mechanism for phase separation that is distinct from bulk MIPS, offering insights into pattern formation in complex active systems.
